newsitem.title: UK: UK broker denies TV allegations in Sumitomo affair.
newsitem.headline: UK broker denies TV allegations in Sumitomo affair.

text.p: British brokers Winchester Commodities Group on Friday denied allegations that a huge copper trading deal arranged by Yasuo Hamanaka had involved his Sumitomo Corp employers paying Winchester inflated prices.

Sumitomo's former star copper trader has pleaded guilty in a Tokyo court to fraud and forgery charges arising out of his metals dealings over 10 years, during which Sumitomo has alleged that he lost it $2.6 billion in unauthorised deals.

A British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC) Panorama television programme on February 17 had quoted documents that it said threw new light on a huge 1993 deal, codenamed RADR, between Winchester and Sumitomo.
It was put together by Winchester, a sophisticated brokerage firm founded in 1991 by traders Charles Vincent and Ashley Levett, and involved nearly 100 inter-related trades.
Panorama quoted an expert on derivatives trading, Desmond Fitzgerald, chairman of Equitable House Investments, as saying Winchester made profits of about $36-$38 million over market prices.
Winchester said in its statement on Friday that it only charged Sumitomo the standard rate of commission, and that the RADR deal was approved by Sumitomo senior management.

"There was nothing unfair about the pricing of the RADR strategy which reflected the enormous risks which Winchester were willing to undertake in respect of the largest derivatives transaction undertaken on the LME (London Metal Exchange) at that time," it said.
"There was no collusion or ring to manipulate copper prices."
The deal was designed to provide a hedge to Sumitomo in respect of their need to buy one million tonnes of copper to satisfy their customers in Asia over two and a half years.
"Winchester as market maker took the other side of the transaction which automatically resulted in an equal and opposite position to Sumitomo".
The statement reiterated that Winchester had nothing to hide and that it had at all times given full cooperation to investigators of the Sumitomo affair.
The statement also referred to a February 17 allegation by the Tokyo prosecutor that Winchester's Tokyo representative paid Hamanaka a gratitude payment worth $120,000.
Winchester said in its statement that the payment was made without the knowledge of Winchester or its shareholders and it noted that no allegation had been made to the effect that it bribed Hamanaka.
